summary: A 1970 note with more comments on the forthcoming protocol, by the same authors as RFC 39. It continues discussion about the proposed host-to-host protocol before it was finalised.

plainLanguage.summary: Still more feedback on rules that were not finished yet, like suggestions on a game before it is released.

questions: more comments on the forthcoming protocol
subtitle: Feedback on three protocol features: error messages, queries, and host status

tldr.problem: The early network protocol was still being designed, and there were open questions about how to handle errors, queries between hosts, and status reporting.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides detailed proposals for three protocol elements: error message formats with classified codes, a query/reply mechanism, and a host status notification system.
tldr.outcome: The feedback influenced the final design of the early Host-to-Host protocol and established patterns for protocol error handling.

today: This early protocol design work established patterns for error handling and status management that became standard in network protocols. The hierarchical error code scheme influenced similar designs in later protocols.

sections.title: Error Message Design
sections.content:
The RFC proposes an error message format with three parts: a code (8-bit field specifying the error type), a command length (16-bit integer in bits), and the command in error (the spurious command itself).

Error codes are categorized into ranges by type: 00 for unspecified errors, 10-0F for resource errors, 10-1F for status errors, and 20-2F for content errors. Specific codes include invalid resource requests, exhausted resources, invalid connection states, unknown commands, and message routing errors. This hierarchical coding scheme allows implementations to handle error classes or specific error types as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An error message tells you what went wrong by using a number code. The numbers are grouped by what kind of problem it is.

sections.title: Query and Reply Messages
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a query message (QRY) that one host can send with its own socket number, and a reply message (RPY) that the receiving host sends back with both its socket and a text response.

The response text contains connection table information: a 16-bit count of relevant entries, followed by entries listing the local socket, foreign socket, link, connection state, flow state, buffer control state, and reconnection control state for each connection. This allows hosts to query each other about which connections are active and in what state.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer can ask another 'What connections do you have?' and the other sends back a list of the connections it knows about.

sections.title: Host Status and Availability
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a NOP (no-operation) message that an NCP sends to indicate its state when it changes to UP. When an NCP recovers from an outage or comes online, it sends a NOP to each remote NCP to announce availability. The sending NCP can build a vector of host statuses from the RFNM (acknowledgment) messages it receives. A receiving NCP can update the availability status of the sending NCP in its own host status table.

This mechanism lets the network collectively track which hosts are currently available, allowing intelligent routing and connection management.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer comes back online, it sends a message to all the other computers saying 'I am here now.' That way, everyone knows which computers are working.
